title: Your First Claude Conversation
description: Have your first meaningful conversation with Claude, learn the basics of effective prompting, and understand how context flows through a conversation.

data.text: The best way to learn Claude is to use it. Start a new chat and try a few different types of prompts. Do not overthink it — Claude is designed to be conversational. You can change direction mid-conversation, ask follow-up questions, and correct Claude if it misunderstands you.
The Anatomy of a Good First Prompt

A good prompt gives Claude three things: context (who you are, what you are working on), a clear task (what you want), and any constraints (format, length, tone). You do not need to be formal or structured — just clear. Compare these two prompts:

data.title: Weak vs. strong prompt
data.content:
Weak: 'Write about dogs.'
Strong: 'I'm writing a blog post for new dog owners. Write a 300-word section explaining why crate training works, using a supportive but practical tone. Assume the reader has never trained a dog before.'

See the difference? The strong prompt tells Claude who the audience is, what to write, how long it should be, and what tone to use.

data.text: Claude remembers the recent conversation — this is called context. Everything you say in a conversation is available to Claude when generating the next response. This means you can refer back to earlier messages, build on previous ideas, and have Claude remember details you mentioned earlier.

data.caption: How conversation context flows through Claude

data.title: Try these in your first conversation

items.text: Ask Claude to explain a concept you know well, as if explaining to a 10-year-old
items.hint: This tests Claude's ability to simplify complex ideas

items.text: Upload a document and ask Claude to summarize it in 3 bullet points
items.hint: Try a PDF, article, or text file

items.text: Ask Claude to help you draft an email you need to send this week
items.hint: Be specific about the recipient and goal

items.text: Have a back-and-forth conversation where you ask Claude to refine something
items.hint: Say 'make it shorter' or 'change the tone to be more formal'

items.text: Try asking Claude to write some code and explain what it does
items.hint: Even if you do not code, this is a great way to see Claude's reasoning

data.text: Claude conversations have practical length limits. In the free tier, conversations are shorter. In the Pro tier, they can be much longer. When a conversation gets very long, Claude may start to 'forget' things from the beginning — this is the context window limit in action. If you notice Claude losing track, start a new conversation and provide a brief recap of the important context.

data.title: Context window in plain language
data.text: Think of the context window like a whiteboard. Claude can see everything written on the whiteboard (your recent conversation). When the whiteboard gets full, the oldest writing fades away. If Claude forgets something you said earlier, it is not because it is 'forgetful' — it is because that part of the conversation has moved off the whiteboard.

data.title: Signs of a productive Claude conversation:
items: You are getting outputs that match what you actually need
You are iterating — refining, not just repeatedly asking the same thing
Claude remembers details from earlier in the conversation
You are surprised by ideas or perspectives Claude suggests
You finish with something you can actually use

data.title: First conversation takeaways
points: Good prompts give context, a clear task, and constraints
Claude remembers recent messages — use that for iterative refinement
Context window limits mean very long conversations may lose earlier details
The best way to learn is by trying different types of prompts
